Teaching a Diffusion World Model to Classify Handwriting

Published on December 17, 2025 • Tags: posts, Machine Learning, World Models

Table of Contents

  • Background
  • Theory
    • From Joint to Conditional: The Score Function Trick

Background

World model agents have been used to achieve state of the art performance on numerous agent benchmarks that require longterm coherence that other models fail on. While something as fancy and cool sounding as a “World model” sounds unapproachable, it is actually quite simple in its most barebones implementation. To show just how simple a world model can be I decided to train the “hello world” of machine learning in the most circuitous manner possible by creating a diffusion based world model to generate the labels 0-9 for samples of handwriting by teaching it to understand the whole universe of handwriting.

Theory

While the idea of a "world model" sounds like a fancy concept that would be technically difficult to approach, the core principle can be demonstrated with basic probability theory. In fact, it can be summarized in three words: "marginalizing over the prior."

From a statistical perspective, you can imagine the most basic MNIST handwriting classifier as simply sampling from the probability distribution of labels conditioned on the image we are trying to classify:

result∼P(label∣image)result \sim P(label \mid image) result∼P(label∣image)

While this framework works perfectly fine for a simple toy problem like MNIST classification, this direct approach has limitations for more complex domains. For example, in reinforcement learning settings like playing Minecraft, you could in principle train a model to sample from:

next action∼P(action∣game state)next\ action \sim P(action \mid game\ state) next action∼P(action∣game state)

However, this behavior cloning approach struggles with compounding errors and lacks the ability to plan or reason about consequences. World models offer an alternative: instead of learning the conditional distribution directly, we learn a generative model of the entire environment and use it to answer conditional queries.

From Joint to Conditional: The Score Function Trick

For our MNIST classifier, this means training a model on the joint distribution of images and labels:

(image,label)∼P(image,label)(image, label) \sim P(image, label) (image,label)∼P(image,label)

At first glance this seems unhelpful - after all, we want to classify images, not generate random image-label pairs. But anyone familiar with Bayes' rule knows we're just a simple transformation away from the classifier we want:

P(label∣image)=P(image,label)P(image)=P(image,label)∑lP(image,l)P(label \mid image) = \frac{P(image, label)}{P(image)} = \frac{P(image, label)}{\sum_{l} P(image, l)} P(label∣image)=​P(image)​​P(image,label)​​=​∑​l​​P(image,l)​​P(image,label)​​

The problem is the denominator. Computing (P(image)) requires summing over all possible labels - and in more complex settings, this marginalization becomes intractable.

This is where diffusion models save the day. Diffusion models learn the score function: the gradient of log-probability with respect to the data being denoised:

sθ(xt,t)≈∇xtlogP(xt)s_\theta(x_t, t) \approx \nabla_{x_t} \log P(x_t) s​θ​​(x​t​​,t)≈∇​x​t​​​​logP(x​t​​)

where xtx_tx​t​​ is the noisy version of our data at diffusion timestep ttt.

Suppose we train a diffusion model on the joint distribution of (image, label) pairs. We can think of our noisy data as (x_t = (image_t, label_t)). The model learns:

sθ(xt,t)≈∇xtlogP(imaget,labelt)s_\theta(x_t, t) \approx \nabla_{x_t} \log P(image_t, label_t) s​θ​​(x​t​​,t)≈∇​x​t​​​​logP(image​t​​,label​t​​)

Now here's the key insight. To sample from the conditional distribution P(label∣image)P(label | image)P(label∣image), consider its score function with respect to the label:

∇labeltlogP(labelt∣imaget)=∇labeltlogP(imaget,labelt)P(imaget)\nabla_{label_t} \log P(label_t \mid image_t) = \nabla_{label_t} \log \frac{P(image_t, label_t)}{P(image_t)} ∇​label​t​​​​logP(label​t​​∣image​t​​)=∇​label​t​​​​log​P(image​t​​)​​P(image​t​​,label​t​​)​​

Since (P(image_t)) doesn't depend on (label_t), it vanishes under differentiation:

∇labeltlogP(imaget,labelt)−∇labeltlogP(imaget)=0\nabla_{label_t} \log P(image_t, label_t) - {\nabla_{label_t} \log P(image_t)}_{= 0} ∇​label​t​​​​logP(image​t​​,label​t​​)−∇​label​t​​​​logP(image​t​​)​=0​​

∇labeltlogP(imaget,labelt)\nabla_{label_t} \log P(image_t, label_t) ∇​label​t​​​​logP(image​t​​,label​t​​)

This is remarkable: our joint model already knows the conditional score function. The intractable normalization constant disappears because it's constant with respect to the variable we're differentiating.

To classify an image, we simply run the diffusion denoising process while holding the image fixed, allowing only the label component to evolve. The model will denoise toward high-probability labels for that specific image—effectively sampling from (P(label \mid image)) without ever computing it explicitly.
